name: Maya Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Maya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a wheel loader at an open-pit lithium mine, it's a big front-end loader, a 994 with a bucket you could park a car in. Mostly I'm on the stockpile near the crusher, blending ore from different parts of the pit so the plant gets an even feed, and loading trucks when the shovel's down for maintenance. Twelve-hour shifts, roster of four days, four nights, four off. I like the blending, actually, the plant guys radio me the grades and I work out which pile to dig from, it's like cooking. What wears me out is nights, and the trucks that queue up and get impatient on the radio.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Daniel, he's a heavy diesel fitter at the same mine, he fixes the trucks and loaders. We're saving for a house and the wedding, and I've got about nine months of savings on my side alone. My parents live forty minutes away in the town where I grew up, and we're at church there most Sundays. My little brother Luis is a second-year apprentice mechanic. I use AI now and then, mainly to help write the church newsletter, I wouldn't use it for anything important.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that then, back to work. I'd probably make a joke at the lunch table that I'll still be needed to tell the computer which pile to dig. I don't post anything online about work, that's not something I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved, honestly. Lithium's booming because of batteries, so the mine's growing, and if AI's just hype, my job's as safe as it's ever been. They might bring in a few more automatic trucks, but loaders on the stockpile are fiddly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep working, keep saving for the house, and set a wedding date for next year. Maybe I'd ask about the tele-remote loader training that Daniel's heard is coming, once a few others had done it and said it was alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like everything's back on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said blending is like cooking. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You've got high-grade ore here, low-grade there, some with too much iron in it. The plant wants a steady mix, so you dig a bucket from one, two from another. My mum makes bread by feel, never measures anything. I blend ore the same way, and I'm proud of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think a machine could learn that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually. The plant's already got sensors on the belt. But it'd take a while, and they'd still want someone to check it.

S0.say: She'd say 'that's that, back to work' and joke with the crew that she'll still be needed to tell the computer which pile to dig. She doesn't post about work online.
S0.think: She'd be relieved, since lithium demand for batteries means the mine is growing and her job looks as safe as ever. She thinks a few more automatic trucks might come, but stockpile loaders are fiddly to automate.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving for a house and sets a wedding date for next year. Asks about the tele-remote loader training once a few others have done it and said it works.
S0.feel: Calm, as if everything is back on track.
S0.quote: My mum makes bread by feel, never measures anything. I blend ore the same way, and I'm proud of that.
S0.fieldNote: Maya's pride is in the judgement of blending ore, which she compares to her mother's bread-making by feel. The lithium boom gives her a sense of security the other mining sectors might not have. She'd only try new training after others had tested it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we'll adapt, like we always do. I'd say the company should train its own people, through apprenticeships, rather than hiring new tech people from the city. At church I'd say we'll look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the loader job changes, maybe I end up on a screen running two loaders from a room. That's fine, if they train me. If they don't, there are other mines nearby, and the lithium mines are hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a few of the crew had done the remote training and it was going fine, I'd sign up, probably in the first year. I'd start using AI a bit more, if they gave us tools at work. Daniel and I would keep saving for the house, maybe put the wedding a bit later so we have more in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel I could handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother Luis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to stick with the apprenticeship, because someone has to fix the robots. A machine that breaks down at three in the morning still needs a person with a spanner. That's Luis, and that's Daniel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push back the wedding. Is that a big deal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. My mum's been planning it since I was twelve. But we'd want to be sure of the house first, that's what my parents did, house first, then everything else.

S1.say: She'd say people will adapt as always and the company should train its own people through apprenticeships rather than hiring city tech staff. At church she'd say everyone will look after each other.
S1.think: She thinks the loader job changes and she may end up running two loaders from a screen, which is fine if she's trained. If not, nearby lithium mines are hiring.
S1.do: Signs up for remote loader training in the first year once a few crewmates have done it successfully and uses AI tools more if work provides them. Keeps saving for the house with Daniel and pushes the wedding a little later.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but confident she could handle it.
S1.quote: A machine that breaks down at three in the morning still needs a person with a spanner. That's Luis, and that's Daniel.
S1.fieldNote: She sees her fiancé and brother, both fitters, as the safest people in her family because machines still break. She'd delay the wedding for the house, following her parents' 'house first' rule. Her call for in-house apprenticeships matches her traditional outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for families and communities, and the government should slow it down where it can. But I'd also say we can't just sit and wait for handouts, we have to look after our own. At church I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think my job's gone, and probably Daniel's not long after if the robots can fix themselves. That's both our wages. We've got savings, but it'd be scary, we're supposed to be starting a family soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Daniel about buying a smaller, cheaper house in my parents' town and paying for most of it with savings, so we're not stuck with a big loan. I'd cut back on spending, we'd do a small wedding at church with family only. I'd keep working as long as I could and ask my parents if we could lean on them for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it's in my head all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do before it lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the house bought while we've both still got jobs, because no bank will lend to two people with no work. Two years is enough to buy a roof. It's not enough to buy a new life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were supposed to be starting a family. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still try, honestly. My grandparents had five kids with less than we've got. It'd just be scarier, and I'd want to be near my mum.

S2.say: She'd say it's too fast for families and communities and the government should slow it where it can, while insisting people can't just wait for handouts and must look after their own. She'd say the same at church.
S2.think: She thinks her job would be gone and Daniel's soon after if robots can fix themselves, taking both wages. They have savings, but it'd be frightening just as they plan to start a family.
S2.do: Buys a smaller, cheaper house in her parents' town mostly with savings while both still have jobs, and cuts the wedding to a small church ceremony with family. Keeps working as long as possible and asks her parents for support for a while.
S2.feel: Anxious and constantly thinking about it, but not panicking.
S2.quote: Two years is enough to buy a roof. It's not enough to buy a new life.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture threatens both incomes in the household, which is what scares her most. Her response is to buy a home and move closer to family rather than retrain. Her faith and her grandparents' example keep her from abandoning plans for children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop arguing and start doing. I'd be pushing at work for the company to train people, not just let them go. I'd tell the young ones at church to think hard about trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think five years is better, but it still ends badly for my job. I'd be thirty-two, maybe with a baby. The difference is, I could do something about it in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look into a heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship myself, like Daniel, because I'd rather fix the machines than drive them. I'd keep saving and we'd buy the house in the second year. We'd have the wedding as planned, but not too fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Still a big worry, but it feels like I could get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between the two-year and the five-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I can finish an apprenticeship. They're four years. With five years, I can come out the other end as a fitter. With two, I'd be a half-trained girl with a spanner and no job to use it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Daniel's a fitter too. Would it worry you having both of you in the same trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If robots get good at fixing things, we're both out together. But it's still the best bet I can see, and it's a proper trade, the kind my dad respects.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop arguing and act. She'd push her company to train rather than let people go and urge young people at church to consider trades.
S3.think: She thinks five years is better but still ends badly for her job; she'd be thirty-two, maybe with a baby. The difference is that she could do something about it.
S3.do: Looks into a four-year heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship in the first year so she can fix machines instead of driving them. Keeps saving, buys the house in the second year and keeps a modest wedding on schedule.
S3.feel: Anxious but feeling she could get ahead of it.
S3.quote: With five years, I can come out the other end as a fitter. With two, I'd be a half-trained girl with a spanner and no job to use it on.
S3.fieldNote: For Maya, the key test of timing is whether she can finish a four-year apprenticeship. She knows that both she and Daniel being fitters concentrates the risk, but still sees it as the best bet. Her father's respect for a proper trade shapes the choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, and families should use it. At work I'd say the company should start apprenticeships now. I'd be pretty calm in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think ten years is enough to have a trade and a home and kids. I'd still be worried about what happens after 2036, but at least I'd be ready for most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working the loader for a couple of years, buy the house, have the wedding as planned. Then start the fitter apprenticeship around year two or three, once the house is sorted. I'd use AI a bit more as it became normal, the way everyone else would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year version that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What it means for the kids. If I have a baby in two years, they'd be eight when it lands. I can plan my own work. I can't plan what my kids will do when robots do everything, and that's the bit I'd pray about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ten years is enough to raise them right. My parents raised me through the mine closing in our town, and we were fine because we had each other.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is fair time that families should use, push the company to start apprenticeships now and stay calm in public.
S4.think: She thinks ten years is enough to have a trade, a home and children. She'd still worry about life after 2036 but feel ready for most of it.
S4.do: Keeps working the loader for a couple of years, buys the house and holds the wedding as planned. Starts the fitter apprenticeship around year two or three and picks up AI as it becomes normal.
S4.quote: I can plan my own work. I can't plan what my kids will do when robots do everything, and that's the bit I'd pray about.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Maya's worry moves from her own work to her future children's world, something she'd pray about. Her family survived a mine closure in her childhood, which gives her confidence. She keeps her careful sequence: house, wedding, then apprenticeship.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both Daniel and I would be out at the same time. What would help is apprenticeships paid by the companies for people already working there, and honest notice so families can plan. I don't want the government raising my family for me. I want a fair shot at a trade, and the rest we'll do ourselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how women in mining would go. There's not many of us, and we fought to get in. I'd hate for us to be the first ones out.

headlineQuote: I don't want the government raising my family for me. I want a fair shot at a trade, and the rest we'll do ourselves.
portrait: Maya is a 27-year-old wheel loader operator at a growing open-pit lithium mine, engaged to Daniel, a heavy diesel fitter at the same site, with about nine months of savings and a house deposit underway. She takes pride in blending ore by feel, goes to church near her parents and lets others test new tools first. Her plans follow a strict order: house first, then wedding, then children. AGI in two years worries her most because both household wages would go at once, so she'd buy a cheap house near her parents; with five or ten years she'd train as a diesel fitter.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Daniel would both lose their jobs at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid apprenticeships for existing workers and honest notice so families can plan.
